title: Documentary Director: There Is No Typical Old Age, Only Specific People
dek: Fan Shiguang, who shot two seasons of Qianlang (前浪), says most marriages end up lukewarm or worse, and growing old together to the very end is rare as hen's teeth; what we lack most isn't stories, it's money, and the willingness to see old people as specific human beings.
why: The first half is the two hosts talking, leaning on feeling; the second half is the director interview with a large number of killed story pitches and behind-the-scenes detail, and the information density is clearly higher — worth starting from 41 minutes in.
who: Listeners following aging, caregiving, family institutions and documentary practice; people in elder care, insurance, legal services and content work can treat the second-half director interview directly as a methodology for finding stories.
skip: 0:11-3:53 opening setup and impressions — you can start straight from the inheritance story at 4:08.

points.h: Five million in inheritance, and the law fights the deathbed wish
points.body: An elderly person in Shanghai with no spouse or children died in a nursing home. Before death she had made a voluntary guardianship notarisation with notary Li Chengyang (李承阳), but had not written a will. While clearing her belongings, the notary found she had left five million in inheritance, including a house, cash and passbooks. The old woman had said many times orally that she wanted to donate it to society and did not want it to go to relatives, but that wish had no legal form. Li Chengyang ultimately chose to follow the law and look for statutory heirs, tracing through archives to children of relatives she had not seen in years. There was disagreement inside the notary office too, with colleagues arguing they should simply respect the old woman's wishes. The compromise was to propose to the inheriting children that 200,000 of the five million be donated to a fund helping old people with no one to rely on; the children agreed.

points.h: Whether they slept together decides whether the inheritance can be given
points.body: An elderly man with a terminal illness gave voluntary guardianship and his estate to a woman who had cared for him for years and was not a relative — and he had a biological daughter. The notary office debated this fiercely, and one key point was whether the two slept together: if they did not, the caregiver was merely a nanny or a live-in housekeeper, and an old man wanting to leave his estate to his nanny seemed acceptable in terms of moral propriety; if there was a sexual relationship, the matter immediately became less proper. The caregiver was herself married, but had had no contact for years, so in effect the marriage did not exist. So it became an open-relationship question, and the notary office did not want to bear the risk of offending public morals over such a judgment.

points.h: Older people finding partners increasingly don't register the marriage
points.body: The protagonist of episode two, Li Kangmei (李康美), was with Lao Li for eighteen years without ever registering the marriage, and there was no de facto marital relationship. The hosts found this far more common than they had imagined: after divorce or the loss of a first marriage, many older people entering a new relationship choose not to marry. They don't necessarily say they love the person deeply; they say they want someone to keep them company, someone to take care of them, and behind that is a fairly deep need against loneliness. Lao Li already had a terminal illness at the time, and Li Kangmei's choice was whether to stay to the last moment or leave early because there was no de facto marital relationship.

points.h: Reality TV forces you to pick a side every five minutes
points.body: The hosts contrast documentary with reality TV: much of the tension in reality TV is manufactured, backed by a very strong narrative — for instance, knowing the audience has views about mama's boys, so they fabricate a mama's boy on screen. This destroys the audience's tolerance for the complexity of real intimate relationships: every plot beat, every five minutes, demands a position, and that position must be the morally most correct one, then projected onto some character, and wherever that character goes you take his side. Documentary works the opposite way: it shows that everyone has it hard, some characters get more screen time and some less, but you can see the difficulty of every one of them, and quite a few of those characters appear pixelated and anonymous.

points.h: The older generation says I sleep badly, not I'm depressed
points.body: Medical anthropologist Arthur Kleinman found that young people today have a rich psychological vocabulary and can quickly say I'm depressed, I'm anxious, I'm a bit bipolar; but even when older people express psychological needs, they still use somatised language — I've been sleeping badly lately, I have a bit of a headache — rather than saying I sleep badly because I think too much, I'm a bit depressed. The hosts explain: in our culture it is easier to talk about physical pain, everyone gets a headache or a fever, there is no stigma; once you talk about depression and anxiety, it is a different order of stigma and suffering.

points.h: The killed pitch: she just wanted to play mahjong
points.body: Director Fan Shiguang (范世广) told a story he himself killed: the most diligent auntie in a hospice ward, whose husband had bladder cancer and not long to live. She took the bus in at seven or eight every morning and left at five or six in the evening, like going to work, but you could see no love on her face — she just asked the doctors and nurses again and again how much longer other people's family members had. Only later did they learn that her son had died of a heart attack two years earlier; she was a shidu family, and her tears had probably run dry two years before. Someone asked what she wanted to do after her husband died, and she said she wanted to play mahjong, because he had never let her play. The first scene shot after the husband died was her finding workers to smash the legs off a two-metre bed one by one with a sledgehammer, and buying a mahjong table to put in that spot. The story was ultimately not used, because the team could not find her real inner world and only grasped part of the facts.

points.h: Growing old together is rare as hen's teeth, not the norm
points.body: Fan Shiguang said the team did fieldwork embedded with roughly fifty families, across the two seasons combined, and found that going from youth to truly growing old together to the very end is not the norm but rare as hen's teeth; most marriages are lukewarm, or even bad. He told of the first season's episode Lovers: an old man with Alzheimer's loses control and hits his wife, the daughter forcibly sends him to a specialised nursing home, and the old woman sneaks off to visit every few days, but the hospital won't let her come because it affects his mood. After the old man is sent to hospital gravely ill, the old woman finally gets her chance to wait on him — cutting his nails, washing his hair, washing his feet. More than a month after he died, the old woman said through tears: I looked down on him my whole life; when we were young I was a good student and he was a poor one, my family were intellectuals and his were workers, he insisted on courting me, and I had no way out, and in the end I muddled through a whole life with him.

points.h: Learning to drive at 95: one sentence strips away the right
points.body: Fan Shiguang said the team worked hard to break stereotypes, because people love to divide into groups and stick on labels — old people are like this, they're just muddled — and there is deep prejudice in that. In season one there was the story of a 95-year-old man learning to drive and taking the licence test; he thought about it and realised he had unconsciously said, "driving is all very well, but he is 95 after all," and then asked himself: in that sentence of mine, 95-year-olds are in fact stripped of their rights — that is, he doesn't deserve it. Public Security Ministry laws and regulations never said a 95-year-old cannot learn to drive, but in verbal violence the right was stripped away. The episode's bullet comments said in large numbers, can this old man really drive on the road, he's so selfish, what if he hits someone — all these worries are built on prejudice.

Because if they did not sleep together, this caregiver is merely, say, a nanny to this terminally ill elderly man, or a live-in housekeeper, that kind of role, and then this old man wanting to leave his estate to the nanny seems acceptable, in terms of moral propriety. But if there is a sexual relationship between the old man and the caregiver, all at once the matter becomes not so proper.
